description: Crimson Atlas is a solo team building a browser-based space mission design game for students. Players pick a mission, design a spacecraft (mass, power, communications, instruments), choose a launch vehicle within budget, and simulate the mission using real physics like delta-v and launch windows. When a mission fails, an AI post-mortem explains which decisions caused it and what would have saved it. Built by a data scientist and ML engineer from Faisalabad, Pakistan.
summary:
Crimson Atlas is a single-player 3D space mission design game that transforms the challenge of reaching Mars into an interactive learning experience. Players design a spacecraft, choose a launch date and landing site, balance six essential resources, and fly their mission from Earth to Mars.

A mission debrief explains the consequences of their decisions and encourages them to redesign and refly. NASA and USGS space data help ground the game in the real world, while its fictional Genesis chapter imagines a long-term human future on Mars.
details:
Space missions are shaped by trade-offs: adding an instrument may improve science, but it can also increase mass, power demand, or cost. Crimson Atlas lets one player take on the roles of a mission team and experience those decisions firsthand.

The player configures a spacecraft, launcher, instruments, communications, and mission duration, then chooses a launch date using an approximate Earth–Mars transfer planner. Six resources—mass, power, budget, data, communications, and time—change with the player's decisions.

The mission continues through launch, stage separation, travel to Mars, orbital scanning, landing-site selection, and descent. After landing, the player deploys a rover, collects science, and sends data back to Earth. A mission debrief explains how decisions affected the outcome and encourages the player to redesign and refly.

The game also includes Genesis, a fictional vision spanning more than 75 years. In Phase 1, robots build a futuristic city on Mars. In Phase 2, CA-1 brings highly skilled people, animals, and species that help support life. In Phase 3, the remaining people travel to Mars.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript power the interface, mission logic, resource management, and scoring. Three.js and WebGL render the 3D mission. NASA and USGS Mars imagery, landing-site coordinates, planetary facts, and approximate planetary positions provide real-world context.

The simulation is designed for education, not real flight planning. Trajectories, budgets, landing physics, and scores are simplified; Genesis is fictional.

Source Code: https://github.com/Mohsin-Irfan/crimson-atlas
